item.title: Georgia jogger runs for her life after stranger allegedly tries to mow her down 3 times
item.description: Jesse Allen Davis allegedly tried to run down a woman three times at a Cobb County apartment complex after she greeted him during her morning workout.
item.content:encoded:
A Georgia woman out for a Sunday morning workout was allegedly forced to run for her life after a stranger tried to mow her down three times moments after she offered him a simple greeting.

The terrifying encounter unfolded at the Sedgefield Apartments in Cobb County on July 19, where the woman was walking and exercising when she crossed paths with Jesse Allen Davis, 21, according to a criminal warrant obtained by Fox News Digital.

The woman did not know Davis, but the two exchanged what authorities described in the warrant as a "brief, polite greeting."

WASHINGTON DRIVER CHASES BOY ON DIRT BIKE DOWN SIDEWALK, GETS HIT WITH MULTIPLE CHARGES

Shortly afterward, Davis allegedly got into his parked 2004 Nissan Sentra, started the car and intentionally drove directly toward the woman at a high rate of speed, according to the warrant.

Another driver pulled into Davis’ path, forcing him to stop before he could allegedly strike the woman, according to the warrant.

The woman fled toward her residence, but Davis allegedly pursued her in his vehicle to the area of Commons Lane before intentionally driving toward her a second time.

She was forced to run onto a sidewalk and seek cover behind a dumpster to avoid being struck, according to the warrant.

WATCH: DRIVER SMIRKS IN MUGSHOT AFTER ALLEGEDLY HITTING GROUP OF CYCLISTS IN CAUGHT-ON-CAMERA ROAD RAGE

But her alleged attacker kept coming.

While the woman remained hidden, Davis allegedly yelled profanities, maneuvered the vehicle and attempted to strike her a third time before fleeing the area, the warrant states.

"He got into a vehicle, and for whatever reason he attempted to strike her with the vehicle while she was in the parking lot," Cobb County Police Sgt. Eric Smith told local outlet WSB-TV.

The woman called 911 while taking cover behind the dumpster, according to the outlet.

SILICON VALLEY DEVELOPER ACCUSED OF MURDER AFTER INVESTIGATORS SAY TESLA REACHED 142 MPH BEFORE FATAL CRASH

"He attempted to strike her with the vehicle two additional times," Smith said.

Davis allegedly struck another vehicle as the incident unfolded, according to a separate criminal warrant obtained by Fox News Digital.

The warrant alleges Davis was driving a gray Nissan Sentra when he collided with a gray Ford Fusion and failed to immediately stop or return to the scene.

WSB-TV also reported that Davis eventually crashed into a pole.

MAN SENTENCED TO 6 MONTHS IN JAIL FOR RAMMING CAR INTO JEWISH GROUP'S WORLD HEADQUARTERS IN NEW YORK

Neighbor Lloydethan White said he witnessed part of the chaos and claimed Davis nearly hit him, too.

"When I had seen him, he almost hit my car and her," White told WSB-TV.

White said he checked on the woman but did not initially realize what she had allegedly just endured.

"I think it’s wrong that a woman has to fear for her life and she’s just trying to go about her normal day and workout," he said.

Davis was arrested and booked into the Cobb County Jail on felony aggravated assault and misdemeanor hit-and-run charges, with jail records listing a total bonding amount of $5,720.

The motive behind the alleged attack remains unclear. Police have not said whether Davis and the woman had any interaction beyond the seemingly innocuous greeting before he allegedly got behind the wheel.

item.title: Joe Scarborough goes scorched earth on Democrats not separating themselves from Hasan Piker
item.description: Joe Scarborough blasts Democrats as "too woke" to condemn Hasan Piker's rhetoric after ally Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan's Senate primary race.
item.content:encoded:
MS NOW "Morning Joe" host Joe Scarborough launched a blistering attack on far-left streamer Hasan Piker and Democrats unwilling to distance themselves from his rhetoric Monday, warning the party risked repeating what he viewed as its costly 2024 mistakes after Piker ally Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan's Democratic Senate nomination.

Scarborough, raising his voice and shouting at times, said Democrats were "too woke to call out the obvious" and questioned why party leaders were reluctant to draw a line over Piker's past comments about rape during Hamas' Oct. 7 terrorist attack, when he remarked that it didn't matter to him if it occurred.

"This is about the Democrats once again, fumbling the football on the two-yard line when they have a chance to make great gains, but being so woke, I don't know if you want to call it woke 1, woke 2, or woke 3, but being too woke to call out the obvious!" Scarborough yelled. "I swear to God. It's really, it's crazy that we're even having this conversation."

The Republican National Committee (RNC) has sought to turn El-Sayed's continued relationship with Piker into a general election liability. RNC national spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre told Fox News Digital Sunday that Democrats' unwillingness to disavow the streamer reflected a broader problem for the party.

MARK HALPERIN CALLS HASAN PIKER A 'HORRIBLE PERSON' AS DEMOCRATS FACE PRESSURE TO DISTANCE FROM STREAMER

"El-Sayed is a terrorist sympathizer and an America-hating socialist. His refusal to distance himself from Hamas-hugging radicals like Hasan Piker reaffirms his true allegiance is to terrorist groups, not America. Democrats' refusal to disavow this clown shows they either share his poisonous ideology or they're too cowardly to confront it," Baldassarre said.

"The Democrat Party is being driven off [a] cliff by socialists who are driving blindfolded while arguing about the view. Unless Democrats hit the brakes, every candidate on the ballot will have to answer for socialists’ outrageous beliefs that will bankrupt our country and strip every American of safety, sanity, and freedom," she added.

Scarborough specifically called on Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., to demand that candidates distance themselves from such rhetoric.

"If somebody says, a woman being raped doesn't matter in the grand scheme of things, it's OK to call that person out and demand that candidates distance themselves from those people!" Scarborough shouted.

FETTERMAN 'DARES' EL-SAYED TO STICK WITH PIKER, CLAIMS MICHIGAN NOMINEE HAS 'LITTLE MAN SYNDROME ENERGY'

The fight has intensified since El-Sayed narrowly defeated establishment-backed Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary. El-Sayed will face Republican Mike Rogers for the seat held by retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.

Piker made repeated appearances with El-Sayed, including at a Detroit pool party the night before the primary. El-Sayed has rejected Piker's most controversial remarks but resisted calls to sever ties.

"Of course I oppose rape. Of course I don't think 9/11 was justified," El-Sayed said during an April appearance on "Fox & Friends." "[Just] because you appear with somebody, doesn't mean you agree with them on everything."

Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., has also challenged El-Sayed to maintain the relationship now that he must appeal beyond Democratic primary voters.

JOHNSON TURNS DEMOCRATS’ SOCIALIST CIVIL WAR INTO NEW WEAPON FOR MIDTERMS

"I dare you to continue to campaign with people like Hasan Piker because he now will quickly find out it’s easy to campaign in the echo chamber as a Democrat," Fetterman told Fox News Digital.

Piker has pushed Democrats in the opposite direction, calling for party members who refuse to support El-Sayed to be "punished," while centrist Democratic group Third Way recently announced a $15 million campaign aimed at weakening the Democratic Socialists of America's influence.

Scarborough said the debate reminded him of Democrats' failure to recognize cultural issues that hurt them during the 2024 election.

"Why are we bringing this up now? We're bringing this up now because it seems an awful lot like what was happening in 2024 when Democrats couldn't get out of their own way to win an election they should have won," he said.

Fox News Digital reached out to the DNC, El-Sayed, Piker and Schumer for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

item.title: Former NFL players call out DiJonai Carrington for blaming ejection on 'white privilege'
item.description: Emmanuel Acho and Breiden Fehoko push back after Dijonai Carrington posted "white privilege" following her ejection for flagrant fouling Sophie Cunningham.
item.content:encoded:
Two former NFL players agree that Chicago Sky guard DiJonai Carrington further impeded racial progress in America by basically blaming her ejection on Saturday on "white privilege."

"This is a prime example of why we can't ever move forward as a country," former NFL player Breiden Fehoko wrote on X about Carrington's accusation.

"For every person who liked this bullsh*t and is encouraging this victim-a** mentality, you should be ashamed. It's honestly sad how far we've drifted as a country."

For background, Carrington hard-fouled Fever forward Sophie Cunningham on Saturday on a play that more closely resembled a clothesline than a play on the ball. Carrington left Cunningham bloodied in the mouth. She was rightfully called for a Flagrant 2 and ejected from the game.

Moments later, Carrington posted "white privilege" on Threads from the locker room, as if racism was the reason for her ejection.

EX-ESPN HOST SAYS SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM DESERVED TO BE EJECTED AND PUNISHED — NOT DIJONAI CARRINGTON, WHO CLOTHESLINED HER

Former NFL player and podcaster Emmanuel Acho also pushed back on the claim.

"DiJonai Carrington posted ‘White Privilege’ from the locker room after being ejected for fouling Indiana Fever’s Sophie Cunningham," Acho wrote on X, reacting to a screenshot of Carrington’s post. "Judge for yourself, but color didn’t have nothing to do with the flagrant 2. IMO."

He continued on his podcast:

"Can we stick to basketball for a moment? She flagrantly hit Sophie Cunningham in the head ... the refs made the right call."

"Now, I'd be remiss if I didn't mention .. this was not a race-based decision. To call that a white privilege-based foul is to completely undermine the term of white privilege and to also completely ignore the rules in basketball. You hit her in the head. You drew blood. You didn’t connect with the ball at all whatsoever.

"So to me, it was just very ignorant and, to some degree, asinine by D.J. Carrington to suggest that that call was based on white privilege. Have we seen examples of white players make that same foul and get away with it? Have we seen examples of black players make that same foul and get away with it? Yes. There was no white privilege involved in that specific call."

Well said.

You can watch the full segment from Acho here.

WNBA FACES DISCIPLINE DILEMMA AFTER CARRINGTON'S 'WHITE PRIVILEGE' POST TARGETING INDIANA FEVER

While Acho and Fehoko are covering the matter honestly and with reason, most of the media is not. Earlier on Monday, OutKick documented some of the most cringeworthy remarks in defense of Carrington.

Most notably, former ESPN anchor Cindy Brunson argued that Sophie Cunningham was the one who deserved to be ejected – not Carrington, who clotheslined her.

You read that correctly.

Elsewhere, the WNBA pregame shows on NBC and ESPN have avoided discussing Carrington's post. In fact, NBC host Maria Taylor didn't just ignore it, but accused those criticizing Carrington of injecting her into the "culture war," as if she played no role in doing so.

The race-lady duo of Jemele Hill and Cari Champion also, predictably, rushed to Carrington's defense.

As we explained, members of the sports media cannot bring themselves to cede an inch of ground in the culture war. That means never, under any circumstances, criticizing a black lesbian in defense of a straight white woman.

Good for Acho and Fehoko for not subscribing to this worldview.

Carrington deserved to be ejected. She deserves to be suspended. And neither has anything to do with race.

item.title: 100 Kodiak driverless trucks are headed for public roads
item.description: Atlas Energy Solutions plans to grow its Kodiak driverless truck fleet from 28 to 100 by mid-2027, with public highway driving in Texas and New Mexico.
item.content:encoded:
Atlas Energy Solutions is expanding its fleet of Kodiak-powered driverless trucks across Texas and New Mexico. The trucks already haul sand to oil and gas well sites without anyone inside the cab.

Now, Atlas and Kodiak plan to grow the fleet from 28 driverless trucks to 100 by mid-2027. They also expect the trucks to begin operating on public roads in early 2027. However, that timeline still depends on operational milestones.

The expansion gives us a clearer look at how driverless trucking could move from private industrial roads onto highways.

Atlas previously operated its driverless trucks from one load-out location at a time. It now runs them simultaneously from two depots about 90 minutes apart. One site is in Texas while the other is in New Mexico. The wider footprint lets Atlas reach more well sites across the Permian Basin. It can also respond faster when customers need more sand delivered. The operation connects with Atlas' 42-mile Dune Express conveyor system. That system moves sand closer to the well sites before the trucks complete the final portion of the trip.

Don Burnette, founder and CEO of Kodiak, said the two companies have built the world's largest fleet of driverless big-rig trucks: "Together, Atlas and Kodiak have deployed the world's largest fleet of driverless big-rig trucks. We've demonstrated that autonomous trucking is delivering meaningful results today. Our expanding partnership, which now covers two unique locations, is creating a blueprint for how autonomy can transform logistics by improving efficiency, increasing productivity, and delivering lasting value for customers at commercial scale."

As of March 31, 2026, Atlas's driverless program operated 28 driverless trucks across 15 routes. Those trucks had carried about 7,000 loads and hauled more than 450,000 tons of sand. The fleet also logged more than 23,500 driverless operating hours during the first quarter of 2026. On July 20, Kodiak-powered trucks delivered 176 loads in one day. The companies called it a daily record for the 18-month deployment.

Earlier in 2026, Kodiak and Atlas also introduced a driverless truck that can pull three connected trailers. The combined loaded weight tops 135 tons. That kind of load would grab anyone's attention. It also raises an obvious question. What happens when these trucks leave private roads and begin driving beside the rest of us?

Kodiak plans to launch driverless highway operations by the end of 2026. Atlas expects its Kodiak-equipped fleet to follow onto public highways in 2027. The company is not alone in moving toward humanless highway freight. A separate autonomous truck recently completed a 230-mile commercial delivery in Texas with nobody in the cab.

Burnette told CyberGuy that other motorists should not expect unusual behavior from Kodiak-powered trucks: "Kodiak-powered trucks already operate autonomously on highways across the southern United States with a safety driver in the cab to oversee the system.The Kodiak Driver is engineered to be a safe and cautious driver and to follow normal driving etiquette, so other motorists should not notice anything unusual."

That may sound reassuring. Still, most drivers will want more than a smooth lane change before they feel comfortable beside a truck with no human behind the wheel. CyberGuy recently took a closer look at whether autonomous trucks can make highways safer, including Kodiak's arguments about fatigue, distracted driving and real-world testing.

The Permian Basin can be brutal on vehicles. Trucks can face triple-digit temperatures, dust storms, sudden flooding and high crosswinds. Dense morning fog can also make visibility difficult. Kodiak equips its trucks with a sensor suite built around cameras, with radar and lidar support. These systems give the truck a detailed view of the surrounding environment.

However, more sensors cannot make every condition safe. Burnette said the truck will stop instead of pushing through dangerous weather: "And if conditions aren't safe, the truck won't keep driving. It slows down and safely pulls over." Kodiak says its system responds to construction zones and emergency vehicles as part of normal driving. It also adjusts to changing road conditions. Severe fog or other hazardous weather can still stop an autonomous trip. According to Burnette, Kodiak-powered vehicles will remain parked when conditions become unsafe.

AI KILL SWITCH BILL COULD SHUT DOWN ROGUE MODELS

A damaged component or communications failure can create a serious problem in any large truck. The stakes may feel even higher when nobody is sitting in the cab. Burnette said the Kodiak Driver checks both the truck and its autonomous system while it operates: "The Kodiak Driver continuously monitors the truck and its autonomous driving system. If it detects a critical problem, such as a mechanical, sensor or communications failure, it can execute a fallback maneuver that safely pulls the truck out of traffic and brings it to a stop in a safe location."

According to Burnette, "The health and safety of all trucks are overseen by Kodiak's command center, and a human can remotely provide assistance should a truck need additional help."

Kodiak also cites a safety evaluation from Nauto, an AI-powered fleet safety company. The Kodiak Driver earned a VERA safety score of 98 out of 100. That result tied for the highest score among more than 1,000 commercial fleets in Nauto's network. The other fleets used human drivers. The system earned a perfect score for inattentive driving and high-risk driving. It also earned 100 for traffic violations. Its aggressive driving score was 95. You can read CyberGuy's full breakdown of the Kodiak Driver's independent safety score. Burnette pointed to the evaluation in his response: "We are proud that an independent evaluation by Nauto, a leader in AI-powered fleet safety technology, gave Kodiak the highest score in a safety study, tying for first place and outperforming 1,000 human-driven fleets."

Driverless trucks create another concern that has nothing to do with rain or road debris. A connected vehicle can become a cybersecurity target. Kodiak does not publicly detail every safeguard. Publishing a complete security blueprint could help attackers. Burnette said Kodiak treats cybersecurity as part of its safety work: "Cybersecurity is something we take extremely seriously because safety starts long before a truck ever reaches the road."

He said Kodiak uses multiple security layers and continuously watches for suspicious activity. The company also tightly limits access to its systems. "We build multiple layers of security into our vehicles and systems to help protect against unauthorized access, and we continuously monitor for unusual activity. For security reasons, we don't discuss the specific safeguards we use or how they're implemented. But access to the systems is tightly controlled and if it detects something unusual, it will bring itself to a safe stop rather than continuing to operate." Kodiak's public technology materials say the company isolates safety-critical functions from external communication ports. It also says it protects vehicle infrastructure with end-to-end encryption.

You probably will not wake up tomorrow and find every delivery truck driving itself. Early public deployments will likely focus on routes where operators already understand the conditions. Still, the Atlas expansion shows that fully driverless trucking has entered commercial service. These trucks are already working without a person in the cab.

The next major step will bring them onto roads used by commuters and families. Other truck drivers will also begin sharing lanes with autonomous rigs. For you, the biggest issue is how the system responds when normal driving suddenly becomes abnormal. Dangerous weather can change a trip in seconds. So can equipment failures, cyberattacks or unpredictable motorists.

Kodiak says its system will reduce speed and move toward a safe stop when conditions become unsafe. Human teams will also monitor the fleet through a command center. The technology could eventually affect deliveries and transportation costs. It may also change trucking jobs, an issue CyberGuy explored in a closer look at whether autonomous trucks could replace drivers by 2027.

As these vehicles reach public highways, transparency will become even more important. Drivers deserve clear information about crash reporting and emergency response. They also need to understand the limits of remote assistance. Regulators will need to test company safety claims against real-world results. A strong safety score provides a starting point, but public trust will depend on consistent performance over time.

OUR ENEMIES FOUND A WEAKNESS IN ESSENTIAL TECHNOLOGY. WE MUST FIX IT … FAST

Kodiak and Atlas are rapidly expanding a commercial driverless truck operation that already moves heavy loads without anyone in the cab. The plan to grow from 28 trucks to 100 by mid-2027 shows how quickly autonomous trucking can scale inside a demanding industrial environment. Public highway use will bring a new level of scrutiny. Drivers will want answers about severe weather, system failures, public-road emergencies and cybersecurity. Kodiak says its trucks can stop when something goes wrong. Human teams also remain available through a command center. However, the technology must prove that those protections work reliably as more trucks enter service. The expansion could reshape how companies transport essential materials. Yet public trust will depend on what happens when these trucks encounter the unpredictable moments every driver knows too well.

item.title: 3 things to avoid in middle age could mean 13 more years without dementia, study finds
item.description: NYU Langone Health research reveals how avoiding high blood pressure, diabetes, and smoking in midlife could add nearly 13 dementia-free years.
item.content:encoded:
Middle-aged adults who manage to avoid high blood pressure, diabetes and smoking can gain nearly 13 additional years of life free from dementia, according to new research led by NYU Langone Health.

The study, published in the journal Neurology Open Access, analyzed long-term health data to determine how midlife cardiovascular wellness shapes brain function decades later.

Minimizing these three common vascular threats between ages 48 and 68 dramatically postpones mental decline, according to the research.

ALZHEIMER'S BLOOD TESTS MAY PREDICT SYMPTOMS YEARS IN ADVANCE, BUT EXPERTS URGE CAUTION

"Our findings argue that people need to actively avert these factors in midlife as a strategy for preserving brain health for more than a decade," said Dr. Josef Coresh, the study’s senior investigator and founding director of the Optimal Aging Institute at NYU Langone, in a press release.

Identifying actionable ways to stall memory loss is vital, he said, pointing out that roughly 42% of Americans are projected to develop dementia after turning 55.

The reviewed data came from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study, an ongoing trial that began in 1986. It included a cohort of more than 12,000 dementia-free participants whose average age was 56.

POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY HELP PROTECT AGAINST A DEADLY DISEASE, DOCTOR SAYS

After screening subjects for smoking habits, elevated blood pressure and diabetes, researchers tracked their health trajectories for an average of 26 years.

By the end of the observation window, 3,008 participants had developed dementia, while 5,238 died without cognitive impairment.

The study revealed a significant gap based on midlife health: Participants who avoided all three risk factors averaged 30 dementia-free years following their baseline exams. In contrast, those with all three conditions averaged just 17 years before developing dementia or dying.

Demographic trends were reported across sex and race. Female participants had longer periods of cognitive health than male participants, regardless of health risks.

Among subjects with all three risk factors, women survived an average of 18.1 years without dementia, compared to 16.6 years for men.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

White participants with all three risk factors averaged 19.6 dementia-free years, while Black participants facing the same health profile averaged 16.0 years.

"These results suggest that vascular risk reduction may benefit all groups, but that certain populations, such as Black adults, may especially benefit from targeted prevention efforts," Coresh said, expressing hope that the data will motivate people to quit smoking and monitor cardiovascular health starting in their late 40s.

The authors noted several limitations to their findings, including that the observational design cannot prove direct cause and effect.

Additionally, health status was recorded during a single visit, and some potential midlife lifestyle changes were unreported.

item.title: Tim Walz's golf game leaves the internet in shock, the NFL is already dunking on the NBA & Kristin Cavallari!
item.description: Tim Walz's golf swing video raises questions as the governor rocks a quarter-zip with no undershirt at a Minnesota course during a two-putt bogey.
item.content:encoded:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday–Friday on OutKick.com.

Here we are. A new week! We've reached the double-digits of August.

Weren't we just saying that about July? Time flies when you're dealing with the WNBA!

What a weekend for that league, huh? They bloodied Sophie Cunningham then declared white privilege. Can you believe it? Of course you can!

Just wait. We're about a day away from the Carrington girl talking about all the racist messages she's received via social media. I'm telling you. It's coming. They have a playbook, and it's right on schedule right now.

Anyway, enough about that league. They're meeting this week to figure out what a "woman" is. They've got enough to deal with!

Welcome to a Monday Nightcaps — the one where Tim Walz throws on a quarter-zip and plays golf at what appears to be a $25-per-round local muni in Minnesota.

PRESIDENT TRUMP RECEIVES BIG CHEERS FROM SPECTATORS DURING LIV GOLF EVENT AT HIS NEW JERSEY CLUB

Wait till you see this swing!

What else? I've got a couple wild catches in the world of baseball — including an honest question about the Savannah Bananas — and the NFL checked back in last week and put up a ratings number that rivals the Daytona 500.

In the HALL OF FAME game! The King is back, boys and girls. Playtime is over.

OK, shut your computer off and take a nap to honor Congress' favorite day — National Lazy Day! — and settle in for a Monday 'Cap.

Yes, today is actually National Lazy Day. The jokes write themselves. I won't make any, because they're all too easy, but you can probably figure it out.

Anyway, let's go ahead and get this week started with everyone's favorite governor!

Tim Walz hopped on Elon's Twitter and had the internet play a round of golf with him at Northwest Angle Country Club. He battled about 4 billion flies during the 2-minute clip, but still managed to smoke a ball off the tee and then finish the hole on some gravel with a two-putt bogey.

All in a single quarter-zip.

What a moment:

Incredible. I have so many questions.

For starters, what's the deal with the tee box? Is he teeing off in just straight grass? Is that a driver off the deck? I can't even see the tee!

It literally looks like he's hitting a tee shot out of the rough.

I'm so confused.

The swing itself? Also a bit of a head-scratcher. I'm not trying to hate on Tim Walz here, although I'm obviously not a fan. I've got no problem admitting a liberal has a good golf game ... if said liberal has a good golf game.

This swing from Tim Walz leaves a lot to be desired. No shot that first shot went 220. None. It was a half swing at best with no finish!

Tim said this was the sixth hole. A quick Google search, which was surprisingly difficult for a golf course, shows me the sixth hole is a 261-yard Par-4. Walz says he has 100 yards in on his second shot.

That would put his drive at 161 yards. Not quite 220, but that's what Learning Center math gets you, I reckon.

The icing on the cake of this whole thing is the quarter-zip with no undershirt. Diabolical move by the governor. Absolutely psycho behavior. I'm not sure I've ever seen that before on a golf course.

I pull off that look once in a while at home, but only at night when it's all I have in the dresser because we're three weeks behind on laundry. Not sure I'd ever go out on an actual golf course rocking that look. Wild stuff.

Anyway, congrats on the bogey, Tim! Onward.

SUPER BOWL CHAMP RUSSELL WILSON TAKES SWING FOR SAVANNAH BANANAS

Moving on ...

I've got an honest question for anyone in class today about the Savannah Bananas ...

All I see on my timeline are these insane plays by Banana Ball players. It's constant. Every week, it's something new.

Do these guys ever screw one of these up? As in, do we just see the good stuff on the timeline, when in reality, they have moments during actual games where they try this stuff and it just doesn't work?

I find it hard to believe that they've never screwed up one of these trick plays. It's almost impossible. So, has anyone here A) been to a game, and B) seen someone completely botch a play? Let me know!

OK, let's rapid-fire this Monday class into a big Monday night. First up? Here's an actual catch from an actual game over the weekend, for those pining for some real baseball:

You know, I've always thought that was a decent strategy for an outfielder. Instead of going all out to make an improbable catch, try to just knock it back into the field of play and see if you can grab it on the way down.

I've never seen it actually work in real life, until Mark Coley II pulled it off over the weekend. 10/10. No notes. Excellent baseball play, excellent baseball IQ. Well done.

Next? The NFL returned last Thursday for the Hall of Fame game and reminded America that we are, in fact, ruled by a King:

Lordy. Seven million! For the HALL OF FAME game. Do you understand how insane of a number that is? You don't?

How's this for a stat:

The NBA averaged 6.35 million viewers for all playoff games across ABC, ESPN, Prime Video, NBC and Peacock this past season. It was the league’s best figure since 1998.

The NFL's most useless preseason game (aren't they all?) surpassed it.

Goodness gracious.

OK, that's it for today. Good class, everyone. Good start to the week.

Here's Kristin Cavallari wrapping up her summer with a bang to take us home.

What's the verdict on Tim's golf game? Email me at Zach.Dean@OutKick.com.

item.title: 'Inmate hopping' influencer who allegedly had relationships with up to 75 inmates avoids jail
item.description: Ash Trevino avoided jail after pleading guilty to welfare and healthcare fraud despite alleged ties to 50-75 Texas Department of Criminal Justice inmates.
item.content:encoded:
Good news for the inmates locked up in the Texas Department of Criminal Justice. An influencer who was alleged to have been involved in relationships with as many as 75 inmates has avoided jail herself.

According to TMZ, who obtained court documents involving a welfare fraud case involving influencer Ash Trevino, prosecutors allege she had relationships with "50-75 inmates of the Texas Department of Criminal Justice."

When the 37-year-old was arrested last December on warrants related to financial crime allegations, it was reported by Complex that she had more than 500,000 followers between Snapchat and Instagram.

FORMER PRISON GUARD WHO HAD SEX TAPE WITH INMATE GO VIRAL IS FILLED WITH REGRET & NOW FOCUSING ON BEING A MOM

The outlet also pointed out that most of the content she made centered around dating incarcerated men or men who had recently been released from prison, something they reported Trevino referred to as "inmate hopping."

These lonely men, some of whom are locked up on charges including aggravated robbery and murder, according to prosecutors, don't have to worry about this particular influencer going silent.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK CULTURE COVERAGE

After being arrested, she posted bond and was released until March of this year, when she was taken back into custody for violations of the conditions of her bond. Prosecutors claimed she drank and purchased alcohol.

While they're not happy about what they describe as "panhandling" on TikTok and allegedly engaging in sexually explicit videos on social media, last week prosecutors did receive a guilty plea from Ash Trevino.

She will avoid jail time after pleading guilty to welfare fraud and healthcare fraud, reports TMZ. She's instead serving two years of community supervision.

On top of that, the "inmate hopping" influencer has to perform 120 hours of community service. She has to complete an anti-theft program, receive financial counseling and pay $16,799.95 in restitution to the Texas Health and Human Services Commission.

But it sounds like she's free to continue her alleged relationships with inmates and add to the 50 to 75 she's already been accused of having relationships with. Romance is out there if you know where to look.

item.title: Bryson DeChambeau addresses Donald Trump meeting with Saudi PIF head at LIV Golf event: having 'conversations'
item.description: Bryson DeChambeau says Yasir Al-Rumayyan needed to have conversations with Trump at LIV Golf New York, raising questions about the tour's future.
item.content:encoded:
To say that it's been a year of turmoil around LIV Golf would be a massive understatement.

The breakaway golf tour was upended earlier this year when the Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF), announced they would pull financial backing for the tour after the end of the season. Given the extremely high prize pools most tournaments offer, as well as individual contracts for players, they have raised legitimate concerns about the future of the league.

Some players started scrambling for pathways out, while others reaffirmed their commitment to LIV. Or at least, not returning to the PGA Tour.

LIV GOLF'S END MAY BE IMMINENT AFTER REPORT SIGNALS SAUDI ARABIA IS PREPARING TO CUT OFF FUNDING

Several events have been canceled, with the stop in New Orleans the first casualty, as well as the team championship event that was scheduled in Michigan. This past weekend however, the LIV Golf New York event at Trump National Bedminster went off as expected, with Joaquin Neimann winning the tournament, and Jon Rahm clinching the league's individual championship.

That wasn't the most notable thing that happened over the past weekend, however. President Donald Trump attended the final day on Sunday, receiving cheers from the crowds. More importantly though, he was reportedly seen talking with Saudi PIF head Yasir Al-Rumayyan and legendary golf star Gary Player. Per Golfweek, the three also met with some LIV players.

While LIV CEO Scott O'Neil has lined up mysterious, unnamed potential investors, it's notable that the Saudi PIF head is still around the events. This despite their decision to end financial support for LIV. After the tournament, Bryson DeChambeau addressed it, saying that Al-Rumayyan wanted to have "conversations" with President Trump.

"I think we all found out last night that he was going to be out here," DeChambeau explained in his press conference.

"I think he needed to have some conversations with the president. That was a whole 'nother' thing. I'm not going to get involved with that."

DeChambeau also said that he was glad to see Al-Rumayyan back at an event and that the PIF has done "wonders" for golf.

"But it was great to see him out here," DeChambeau continued. "I think he's done wonders for us and the global game of golf. I think there's a great place for the PIF and where they want to be moving forward.

LIV GOLF CEO QUIETS SPECULATION WITH ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW INVESTOR TO KEEP CIRCUIT AFLOAT INTO 2027

"Where that is, I'm not exactly sure. I have no idea. But I know that he's supported golf for a long, long time, and as this transitions over hopefully, into the new investor's hands and into the players' hands, we really have an opportunity to align a lot of the global incentives to be a force for good for the game."

DeChambeau also spoke about his conversation with Trump after the round, which was mostly complimentary about the course itself and how well players are treated at Trump-owned courses.

"I told him how tough his golf course is. I got my butt kicked this week, that's for sure," he said.

"That was really all we talked about. Whenever we go to the properties, they've been great to us. The hospitality is amazing. They treat us well. All their staff are amazing."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Trump has always been a big supporter of professional golf, as well as the LIV Tour specifically, but it's unclear whether he was helping to mediate some type of negotiation with LIV personnel and the PIF, or whether their conversations were entirely unrelated to golf. Despite the new funding announcement, there are still plenty of major issues to address for O'Neil and prominent stars like DeChambeau. Massive guarantees for Jon Rahm and others, whether they can continue the elevated purses they've offered, the format of the tour going forward, how many players will be involved...just to name a few.

Seems like there's plenty more coming from this meeting.

item.title: Conservatives shred AOC as she attempts to brush off radical 'Woke 1' wave amid 2028 speculation
item.description: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez dismissed woke policies as a past phase, but conservatives are now demanding accountability for years of DEI activism.
item.content:encoded:
Conservatives online aren't willing to forgive and forget the destruction caused by woke activists over the past several years after Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., flippantly cast aside the behavior as a thing of the past.

AOC, an original member of the so-called Squad of progressives elected to Congress in 2018, brushed off in a Sunday morning interview the first wave of 'woke,' which she helped champion.

"You don't get to spend years pushing to fundamentally transform the country, divide it on racial lines, inject DEI into every institution, and then try to brush it off as a minor misunderstanding when your worldview turns out to be extremely unpopular with the American people," said Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, on X in response to her comments.

ALEXANDRIA OCASIO-CORTEZ SHRUGS OFF PAST 'DEFUND THE POLICE' COMMENTS, JOKING 'WOKE 1 WAS CRAZY'

ABC "This Week' host Jonathan Karl briefly pressed the congresswoman, who is a member of the New York chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), on radical comments made by fellow socialist and Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong in 2020 and 2021.

"I have a local city councilman that has this saying, 'Woke 1 was crazy,'" Ocasio-Cortez said while grinning. "And I think that what’s important is that we have to assess what a candidate is saying now."

But the political right isn't ready to extend an olive branch to proponents of woke-ness like AOC, no matter which version or iteration of the movement they are pushing.

"AOC and the far-left said these issues were existential just a couple of years ago. They said we needed to reorder our entire society and nation around them… " said one X account with more than 350,000 followers. "Now they are laughing it all off, admitting they got swept up and couldn’t think logically. You are not fit to lead."

"Never forget that AOC led Woke 1 charge," said conservative commentator Steve Guest.

HASAN PIKER MAKES AOC HIS 2028 PICK FOR PRESIDENT, SAYS IT'S 'NOT EVEN A QUESTION’

AOC's posts from that time period demonstrate as much, like several where she claimed men could have periods.

"Not just women! Trans men & non-binary people can also menstruate," she tweeted in 2021, earning 64,000 likes on the social media platform. "Some women also don't menstruate for many reasons, including surviving cancer that required a hysterectomy. GOP mad at this are protecting the patriarchal idea that women are most valuable as uterus holders."

In a follow-up post, she wrote: "Trans, two-spirit, and non-binary people have always existed and will always exist. People can stay mad about that if they want, or they can grow up."

"AOC is going to run for president in 2028. Now she’s saying Democrat policies in 2020 era — woke 1 she calls it — were all crazy," said Outkick founder Clay Travis. "Many of us remember being ripped for opposing all these insane policies. Now Dems want to pretend that era never happened."

There is speculation that the four-term congresswoman will throw her hat into the ring for the Democratic nomination for president during the 2028 election cycle. So far, however, she has dodged questions on the subject of her political future.

If she were to launch a bid, it's likely the party would push AOC to shift further towards center left if she wants to earn the backing — and the money that comes with it — of the Democratic National Committee (DNC) and the rest of the Democrat establishment.

"Democrats think they can brush this off without actually conceding anything. 'Wow man, those 2010s were crazy and 2020 was insane, wasn't it?' You don't get to laugh away the generational enemies you created," said commentator Christian Heiens.

"Does calling Woke 1 crazy mean you now oppose any of the ideological positions that Wokeism demanded of you? Of course not. They haven't changed their minds about anything," he continued. "These things have come to define the Left at this point. No Democrat can oppose them without losing their primary."

AOC TAKES PAGE FROM BIDEN PLAYBOOK IN DODGING INTERVIEWS WITH NATIONAL PRESS

Other online critics called for further explanation about what qualities of "Woke 1" Democrats like AOC now oppose that they once publicly supported.

"If you’re going to go with the line 'Woke 1 was crazy,' I think we need a bit fuller of an account of why you and these other politicians became crazy and what you all learned about how not to do it again," said Josh Barro, who bills himself as a political centrist.

Fox News Digital reached out to AOC's office for comment, but did not hear back at time of publication.

item.title: Ben Jones, 'Dukes of Hazzard' actor and former congressman, dead at 84
item.description: Ben Jones, who played mechanic Cooter Davenport on "The Dukes of Hazzard," died from a heart attack at age 84, his wife announced.
item.content:encoded:
"The Dukes of Hazzard" star Ben Jones has died. He was 84.

The actor appeared as "good ol' boy" mechanic Cooter Davenport in the beloved series from 1979 to 1985.

Jones had a "massive heart attack" at his home Sunday in Washington, Virginia, as he was waiting to watch his beloved Atlanta Braves play baseball, his wife, Alma Viator, said on social media. The couple had been married since 1992. 

Rappahannock County Sheriff Connie Compton also confirmed his death.

Viator wrote on Facebook, "I lost the love of my life today. Ben passed from a massive heart attack. He was home resting in his favorite chair waiting for the Braves to come on and whoop the Yankees."

"Ben had the most amazing rich full life. He loved and was loved by so many. He will be missed. I love him so so much," she finished off her post.

Viator shared the news along with an image of Ben holding a dog.

Jones was born in Edgecombe County, North Carolina on August 30, 1941.

‘KNOTS LANDING’ STAR DONNA MILLS SAYS REFUSING TO POSE NUDE COST HER PLAYBOY COVER

He got his start on stage, before making his film debut in 1972 for "Together For Days" as Douglas. He also appeared in "Moonrunners" in 1975 as Fred and "The Lincoln Conspiracy" in 1977.

On the TV front, Jones made his television debut in 1976, playing a thief in an episode of "Movin’ On."

He also appeared in the 1977 series "Nashville 99," and "The Magical World of Disney" in 1978.

Jones landed the role of Cooter Davenport in "The Dukes of Hazzard" in the seventies.

‘DALLAS' STAR LINDA GRAY REVEALS THE BIZARRE WAY LARRY HAGMAN AVOIDED KISSING SCENES 

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

He played Davenport for more than 140 episodes from 1979 to 1985.

He reprised his role as Davenport in "The Dukes of Hazzard: Reunion!" in 1997 and "The Dukes of Hazzard: Hazzard in Hollywood" in 2000.

His final TV appearance was in "Surface" in 2005, and his final film he appeared in was the 2021 movie "Unbreakable."

In addition to his acting career, Jones also had a political career.

ANN-MARGRET, 85, REVEALS THE HABIT THAT KEEPS HER FEELING FOREVER YOUNG

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Jones served two terms in the House of Representatives.

He served as a U.S. House of Representatives member from Georgia’s fourth district from 1989 until 1993.

Jones’ "Dukes of Hazzard" co-star Tom Wopat shared a statement to Fox News Digital, and also shared it on his Instagram on Sunday.

Wopat, who played Lucas K. "Luke" Duke, said: "’The Dukes of Hazzard’ lost another integral part of their cast today. Ben Jones was a fine friend and a fierce advocate of all the best things we can offer in the entertainment business. He will be sorely missed… Denver Pyle frequently said to Ben, ‘I’m not your Uncle Jesse!’ But I feel like we lost a Duke cousin today."

Whey Jennings, grandson of country music legend Waylon Jennings, is also grieving the loss of his dear friend and musical supporter. The two shared the stage on multiple occasions, but their bond extended well beyond performing together. Jones also helped finance Jennings’ first recorded live album, playing a meaningful role in the singer-songwriter’s career.

"Wow, this one hurts," Jennings told Fox News Digital. "I'll never forget all you have done for me, brother. It's been an honor to share the stage with you so many times. Thank you for believing in me. You have been a true friend when I needed one most, and I'm gonna miss you so much. I love you, Ben. Alma, I love you very much. Big hugs and prayers."

The show and Cooter lived on because it was funny, had plenty of action and car chases and had a good, family-friendly heart, Jones previously told the Richmond Times-Dispatch in 2001.

"The show reflects the values of the heartland of America. The good guys always win," Jones said.

item.title: El-Sayed disavows Hasan Piker's 9/11 comments but decries 'cancel culture'
item.description: Abdul El-Sayed called Hasan Piker's 9/11 remarks dumb but complained about cancel culture when NBC pressed him on their campaign association.
item.content:encoded:
Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said far-left streamer Hasan Piker's 9/11 remarks were "dumb" on Sunday, but said the country was "so stuck" in cancel culture when confronted about his association with the internet personality.

NBC's Kristen Welker asked El-Sayed on "Meet the Press" if he would welcome Piker on the campaign trail, as he's already campaigned with him prior to winning the state's Senate primary over moderate Haley Stevens. Piker also attended El-Sayed's victory party and called for Democrats who oppose the Michigan Senate candidate to be "punished."

El-Sayed dodged and said he was more concerned about who he was campaigning for and beating Republican candidate Mike Rogers.

"When asked about Hasan Piker's comments on 9/11, Sen. Bernie Sanders called it a dumb statement. Do you agree? Do you disavow those comments that America deserved 9/11?" Welker pressed further.

HASAN PIKER STANDS BY 'INTENTIONALLY PROVOCATIVE' CLAIMS THAT HAMAS IS 'A THOUSAND TIMES BETTER' THAN ISRAEL

"Of course it was a dumb statement and, of course, I think Hasan himself would say that was a dumb statement," El-Sayed told Welker. "He disavowed it. So yes, America didn’t deserve 9/11, but you know, to sit here and play gotcha politics with a dumb thing somebody said out of context that they disavowed themselves — to say, ‘Ah well, what does that mean about what you think?’" 

"I want to be held accountable for what I say and what I do, rather than this idea that we’re so stuck in cancel culture that all of us agreed was a bad idea back in 2020, but we seem to want to bring back," he added.

Sanders called the comments "dumb" earlier this month in an interview on CNN, but said the Democratic Party should be inclusive of the far-left streamer.

The progressive Vermont senator also cited cancel culture.

"I think that's a dumb statement," Sanders said at the time. "On the other hand, he has a whole lot of followers and a lot of things that he's saying that are making sense to a lot of people. I think, you know, we have to get above cancel culture. You know, when you're doing radio, whatever they do, podcasts three hours a day, you say dumb things."

HASAN PIKER'S DEFENSE OF HAMAS HAVING 'RIGHT TO RESIST MILITARILY' DRAWS CONDEMNATION FROM HUMAN RIGHTS GROUPS

Psychotherapist and author of "Therapy Nation," Jonathan Alpert, told Fox News Digital that citing cancel culture seemed like a "dodge."

"El-Sayed clearly knows Hasan Piker’s 9/11 comments were a problem," Alpert said. "He called them dumb. Fair enough. But then he turns around and complains about cancel culture when people scrutinize the relationship. You can’t have it both ways. If the comments are bad enough that you feel the need to distance yourself from them, people are allowed to ask why the association was there in the first place."

"We’ve started calling almost any uncomfortable criticism ‘cancel culture,’" he added. "Sometimes criticism is unfair and sometimes people do get punished simply for holding an unpopular opinion. But getting tough questions about your judgment isn't the same thing."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

He also called El-Sayed's response a "psychological move," and said instead of discussing the criticism, he attacked the criticism and suggested it was unfair.

"Now you’re the victim and your critics are the problem," he said. "Politicians do this all the time."

item.title: Former Arizona Cardinals GM accused of multiple schemes, including one that cost DeAndre Hopkins $13 million
item.description: DeAndre Hopkins accuses Steve Keim of setting him up with a contaminated drug test that cost him $13 million while playing for the Arizona Cardinals.
item.content:encoded:
Former NFL general manager and league executive of the year Steve Keim is being implicated in multiple defamatory schemes, but he has yet to respond to those except to friends and business associates he's communicated with.

Keim, the former Arizona Cardinals general manager, is being accused by former Cardinals player DeAndre Hopkins of somehow setting him up for a failed NFL test that returned positive results for performance-enhancing drugs.

That test eventually led to the Keim and the Cardinals releasing Hopkins in 2023.

"I got set up when I played for his team and lost 13 million," Hopkins wrote in a reply to an Instagram post over the weekend. "Skeme Slime was my GM, contaminated drug test, go figure how that happened."

CARDINALS CUT DEANDRE HOPKINS BUT OTHER TEAMS ARE INTERESTED

Hopkins was suspended for the first six games of the 2022 season after violating the NFL's policy on performance-enhancing substances. An independent expert concluded the banned substance likely came from a "contaminated" supplement, but the NFL upheld the suspension because players are strictly liable for prohibited substances found in their systems.

The suspension had significant financial consequences beyond the six-game NFL penalty. Because his contract contained maximum forfeiture language, the suspension cost Hopkins approximately $13 million in guaranteed money.

The suspension also voided Hopkins' no-trade clause, giving Keim greater flexibility in eventually moving on from the five-time Pro Bowl receiver.

Keim, could not be reached for comment, but has been apparently upset to learn his former player leveled accusations against him for that long-ago incident and apparently answered Hopkins on Instagram.

But both the Hopkins comment and the Keim reply have since been deleted.

Keim was on a flight and unavailable Monday afternoon but he has told multiple NFL people he has no connection to the Hopkins issue.

"It would make no sense to do that to my player," Keim told one source who relayed it to Fox News Digital.

It doesn't end there for Keim, who has other fires to address.

Barron’s reported in mid-July that Keim tied himself to Mohamed Coulibaly, who allegedly authored a scam to cheat NFL players out of hundreds of thousands of dollars by persuading them to invest in fake Shopify stores.

The report went largely unnoticed until Keim's name surfaced publicly in the Hopkins allegations.

Barron's reported that Keim participated in investor calls involving the alleged e-commerce scheme and was even on the so-called pitch deck shared with potential clients for Motion Ventures.

The deck identifies Keim as the chief operation/growth officer for Motion Ventures.

Multiple NFL players have privately told Fox News Digital that they are routinely approached by companies pitching investment opportunities but they typically view these with skepticism.

The problem with the Motion Ventures pitch is apparently that Steve Keim's name being included gave players comfort that a known NFL executive was involved, suggesting the company could be trusted.

No player who spoke with Fox News Digital with the understanding their name not be used alleged they had spoken to Keim directly.

Keim spent time after he left the Cardinals as the general manager of the Klutch Sports talent representation agency football division.

NFL EMPLOYEES’ TROUBLING DRIVING INCIDENTS MOUNT, COSTING JOBS AND PUTTING OTHERS AT RISK

That job banked on Keim using his name recognition and NFL reputation to give the agency's new football division gravitas.

Fox News Digital contacted Klutch Sports for comment but a source said Keim is no longer employed at the agency.

Keim in 2018 pleaded guilty to extreme DUI when he delivered a .93 result in a sobriety test. He was suspended five games and fined $200,000 by the Cardinals with the fine going to Arizona chapters of Mothers Against Drunk Driving.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

After taking an indefinite health-related leave of absence in December of 2022, the Cardinals announced on Jan. 9, 2023, that Keim was stepping down as general manager and that the two sides had mutually agreed to part ways. The announcement came one day after the Cardinals finished a disappointing 4-13 season.

Keim is still welcome in NFL circles. Since the start of training camps around the league, he has being traveling to various practice sites and been talking to general managers and other members of team front offices and coaching staffs.

item.title: Trump bets economic pressure can squeeze Iran as regime’s own failures deepen the pain
item.description: President Donald Trump says he is "low-keying it" with Iran as sanctions and a naval blockade compound Tehran's financial crisis and inflation.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump is signaling, at least for now, he is prepared to let mounting economic pressure on Iran do more of the work rather than immediately expand military action against Tehran.

"We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money," Trump told Axios’ Barak Ravid in a phone interview Sunday. Axios reported Aug. 9 that Trump described the U.S. approach as "low-keying it" and said Iran was in severe economic distress and struggling to pay its troops.

Trump has argued that the U.S. naval blockade on the Strait of Hormuz has compounded Iran’s financial crisis. His comments come after weeks in which the administration repeatedly raised the possibility of renewed large-scale military action. 

But as the administration increasingly points to Iran’s financial distress as leverage, a more complicated question is emerging: How much of Iran’s economic crisis is the result of U.S. sanctions, the war and blockade — and how much stems from decades of corruption, economic mismanagement and spending decisions by the Islamic Republic itself?

IRAN’S DEEPEST WEAKNESS IS GETTING EXPOSED THROUGH AMERICA’S MAXIMUM PRESSURE CAMPAIGN

Trump reinforced the message on Truth Social Sunday, writing that Iran had shown "51 years of bad behaviour" while sharing a graphic depicting the Iranian rial’s steep decline. The graphic was titled "Iran has NO MONEY" and described the currency as "trash."

The economic pressure is increasingly visible in the daily lives of ordinary Iranians. An investigation published by the Iranian newspaper Jahan-e Sanat last week described supermarket workers encountering customers who allegedly shoplifted basic groceries including bread, cheese and meat, or ate packaged food inside stores because they could no longer afford it. The accounts offered a stark glimpse of the strain on Iranian households as prices rise and purchasing power erodes.

Washington, meanwhile, has intensified its campaign against Tehran’s revenue streams. Under what the Treasury Department calls Economic Fury, the administration has targeted Iran’s oil trade, shadow banking networks, weapons procurement operations, cryptocurrency holdings and sanctions-evasion infrastructure. Treasury said June 10 that the campaign had prevented "tens of billions of dollars" in revenue from being accessible to the Iranian regime and its proxies. On July 29, Treasury said OFAC had sanctioned more than 100 vessels linked to Iran’s shadow fleet since the beginning of 2026.

A Treasury spokesperson told Fox News Digital on background that "Economic Fury has left the regime desperate for cash."

"Iran’s economy is in freefall, inflation has skyrocketed, and as President Trump said on Sunday, the regime’s ability to pay its troops has been decimated," the spokesperson said.

WHO IS AHMAD VAHIDI? IRAN’S NEW IRGC CHIEF TIED TO GLOBAL ATTACKS AND ‘DEATH TO AMERICA’ IDEOLOGY

A U.S. official told Fox News Digital on background that the administration still views economic pressure as one part of a broader strategy.

"President Trump has always been clear that he will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon. While he has been consistent in saying he prefers a diplomatic solution, he continues to retain all options if Iran continues to engage in terrorism and refuses to make a deal," the official said.

"The United States is strangling what’s left of Iran’s economy with one of the most successful naval blockades in history – and Iran would be wise to make a deal. Otherwise, they know what will happen."

Miad Maleki, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies and former Treasury Department sanctions official, said the pressure has accelerated Iran’s economic decline, but argued that Tehran’s own policies created many of the underlying vulnerabilities.

"Sanctions and the war have accelerated Iran's economic decline, but both are consequences of the regime's own troublemaking; its nuclear brinkmanship, missile and drone attacks on tankers, and support for terror proxies, not causes imposed on an innocent bystander," Maleki told Fox News Digital.

"It's a government's basic responsibility to provide for and serve its nation — this regime has instead served a failed revolutionary ideology that has produced nothing but suffering for ordinary Iranians," he added.

Maleki said the deeper story can be seen over decades, arguing that even when sanctions eased and oil revenues increased, Iran continued directing significant resources toward its security establishment and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

IRAN’S REVOLUTIONARY GUARD SIDELINES PRESIDENT AS MILITARY GRIP EXPANDS

According to Central Bank of Iran national accounts data provided by Maleki to Fox News Digital, Iran’s military share of total government spending rose from 16% in 1993 to 52% by 2006, while education spending fell from 27% to 15%. Spending on health and social affairs also declined as a share of government expenditures, he said.

Maleki pointed to the 2020 budget as another example of the disparity. The IRGC received approximately $6.96 billion, compared with $2.73 billion for Iran’s larger conventional military, known as the Artesh — roughly 2.5 times as much, according to an analysis published by the United States Institute of Peace’s Iran Primer based on figures from Iran’s parliamentary research center.

"The issue is not simply that Iran spends heavily on defense," Maleki said. "It is that an oil-dependent economy repeatedly directed enormous resources toward the military and the IRGC while basic public services and ordinary households were under increasing pressure."

And the official budget captures only part of that spending. Maleki, citing both his experience at the Treasury Department and outside research, said the IRGC benefits from significant commercial and off-budget resources. A 2017 American Enterprise Institute study estimated that the IRGC’s so-called "gray budget" could add another 50% to 100% to its military outlays.

"Ultimately, the responsibility lies not with external pressure but with structural corruption, chronic economic mismanagement, and spending priorities fundamentally detached from ordinary Iranians' needs and the country's genuine economic potential," Maleki said.

That influence extends far beyond military spending. The IRGC has also built a sprawling economic apparatus that gives it control over major sources of revenue and, critics argue, leaves it particularly well positioned to profit from the opaque channels sanctions create.

Its economic arm, Khatam al-Anbiya Construction Headquarters, became a major force in the Iranian economy after the Iran-Iraq War and expanded across construction, energy and infrastructure. The Treasury Department designated Khatam al-Anbiya in October 2007, describing it as an IRGC engineering arm used to generate income and fund the organization’s operations.

Treasury acknowledged that Iran is increasingly turning to opaque financial channels to circumvent U.S. pressure, but argued that those networks are themselves becoming targets of the campaign.

"The regime is increasingly having to invent new ways to try to evade U.S. sanctions through shadow banking networks, including through exploiting crypto," the Treasury spokesperson said. "Treasury continues to monitor and aggressively dismantle these networks to ensure Iran cannot sustain its campaign of terror and regional destabilization."

On Aug. 7, Treasury announced separate actions against cryptocurrency exchanges it said were being used to finance the IRGC and against international currency networks that it said were moving hundreds of millions of dollars for Iran.

FREED AMERICAN REVEALS BRUTAL IRAN PRISON ORDEAL, WARNS HOSTAGES FACE GREATER DANGER

Morad Tahbaz, an Iranian-American conservationist who spent nearly six years imprisoned in Iran’s Evin Prison before being released with four other Americans in September 2023, said sanctions have effectively created what he described as a lucrative "franchise" for those controlling the channels through which money and goods move.

"They have created a huge franchise for themselves because of these sanctions," Tahbaz told Fox News Digital. "Money can't flow freely to the Iranian government's treasury because of the sanctions. So what happens, everything is like a black market, gray market, illegal smuggling from the oil to everything else coming in and out."

"And of course, the people who are hurt most by all of this are the people of Iran," he added. "They're unfortunately, very unfortunately, taking the brunt of all of these in their daily lives."

Tahbaz said the entrenchment of the IRGC-linked economy may itself complicate efforts to end the confrontation because those profiting from restricted financial channels have an incentive to preserve them.

"They don't want to see the sanctions go away, because they will lose their franchise, if you will," he said. "They will lose their power, their control over the money and everything that goes along with it."

Tahbaz said the economic interests created by the sanctions also help explain some of the internal tensions within Iran. 

"This is the battle going on inside Iran when you hear there is tension within factions," he said. "And I think to see a solution to this war, if you will, we have to look to what's happening in Iran," he said. 

Treasury said it maintains standing authorizations intended to limit sanctions’ effects on ordinary Iranians, including certain humanitarian trade involving agricultural products, medicine and medical devices; noncommercial personal remittances; and communications-related software, hardware and services. OFAC also considers additional requests on a case-by-case basis, the spokesperson said. The authorizations are contained in OFAC regulations and General License 8A.

item.title: Mike Trout golf outing goes from team-bonding event to awkward MLB trade deadline mess for Angels
item.description: Mike Trout's private golf club became the scene of MLB trade deadline chaos as four Los Angeles Angels teammates were dealt mid-round on Aug. 3.
item.content:encoded:
In the midst of the MLB season, when off days are few and far between, players simply have to take what the schedule gives them when it comes to getting out on the golf course. For the Los Angeles Angels, one of those days happened to be August 3, MLB trade deadline day, and with the team on the East Coast, it was as good an opportunity as any to get out to Mike Trout's private club, Trout National.

With the Angels owning a record of 43-69 at the deadline and the front office going full-on sell mode, what was meant to be a stress-free day on the links turned into a complete and total mess.

The Tiger Woods-designed Trout National is a private club with a budget of $100 million located in the 12-time All-Star's hometown of Vineland, New Jersey. The club is the definition of private, with only a select number of golfers stepping foot on the property; therefore, it's fair to assume the dozen teammates Trout welcomed to play were looking forward to the experience.

MLB PLAYER ADLEY RUTSCHMAN'S RED SOX TRADE RUINED 'SPIDER-MAN' MOVIE PLANS WITH ORIOLES TEAMMATES

The excitement didn't last too long, at least for four of the players teeing it up at Trout National.

According to The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal, relievers Ryan Zeferjahn and Brent Suter, along with outfielder Jo Adell, were traded in the middle of their rounds.

Reliever Kirby Yates was lucky enough to get through his round without being dealt, but found out he had been shipped to the Pittsburgh Pirates in a car leaving the course.

Suter, who was in his first season with the Angels, had his priorities in order when he received the call, telling Rosenthal that his first question was, "Can I finish the round? Can I golf?"

The 11-year veteran did get to enjoy a round before a new reality set in as he made his way to a new organization.

Things didn't go as smoothly for Zeferjahn, however, as he found out that he had been traded to the Chicago Cubs during a rain delay with six holes left to play.

There isn't exactly a perfect place to be when finding out you've been traded to a new team, but on a golf course on an off day has to be up there on the list.

FAUCI DISCUSSED COVID MRNA VACCINE CONCERNS FOR PREGNANT WOMEN IN TEXT CHAIN RELEASED BY SENATE COMMITTEE

The release questioned why only three contacts were listed by name, while all other text messages are identified only with phone numbers, among the 34,000 text messages and 522 voicemails.

Murthy initially asked whether there was any reason to favor vaccination earlier or later in pregnancy and whether officials had seen evidence of adverse outcomes among pregnant women who had already been vaccinated.

Fauci, director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases at the time, responded that there were "no data or theoretical reason" to believe vaccination earlier in pregnancy should be preferred over later vaccination. SEN RON JOHNSON TALKS FAUCI EMAILS, NEW SENATE FILIBUSTER STRATEGY ON 'RUTHLESS'

Walensky replied that it was "definitely a good point, esp after dose two." Murthy then wrote that he had been hearing concerns about mRNA causing mutations in a developing fetus and said Fauci’s point about a cytokine response after the second dose was "a really good point."

The following day, after Murthy flagged a World Health Organization recommendation at the time advising against use of Moderna’s vaccine in pregnant women because of limited data, Fauci emphasized that officials had to weigh the potential risks of vaccination against the risks posed by COVID-19 itself.

He wrote that more than 10,000 pregnant women had already been vaccinated with "no issues" reported, that Food and Drug Administration, Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) and American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists guidance allowed pregnant women to choose vaccination, and that animal toxicology studies had not raised red flags.
